deep.reconstruction:
Context: Section 6 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1854, published 1867). Section 5 has just derived the necessary and sufficient condition for Riemann integrability. Section 6 now gives an explicit example of a function that is discontinuous on a dense set but still integrable.

(1) Definition. (x) := x − round(x), the excess of x over the nearest integer, so (x) ∈ (−1/2, 1/2). At half-integers the two candidates are +1/2 and −1/2, and Riemann sets (x) = 0, their mean. The function is f(x) = Σ_{n≥1} (nx)/n².

(2) Convergence. Since |(nx)| ≤ 1/2, the series is dominated by (1/2)Σ1/n². It therefore converges absolutely and uniformly for every x. The step 'wie leicht zu sehen' is filled here by me.

(3) One-sided limits. Each term (nx)/n² has one-sided limits everywhere. By uniform convergence (Weierstrass M-test, my justification) one may pass to the limit termwise. So f(x±0) = Σ (nx±0)/n² exists for every x.

(4) Where the jumps are. (y) is continuous except at half-integers y = (2j+1)/2. There (y+0) = −1/2, (y−0) = +1/2 and (y) = 0.
- Take x = p/(2n) in lowest terms, p odd. Then mx is a half-integer iff m = n·k with k odd (my step).
- Each such term contributes −1/(2n²k²) to f(x+0) − f(x), and +1/(2n²k²) to f(x−0) − f(x).
- Summing over odd k: f(x+0) = f(x) − (1/(2n²))(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + …) = f(x) − π²/(16n²), using Σ_{k odd} 1/k² = π²/8.
- Symmetrically f(x−0) = f(x) + π²/(16n²). The total jump is π²/(8n²).
- At all other x, no term jumps, so f(x±0) = f(x).

(5) Consequences. f is discontinuous exactly at the rationals with even denominator in lowest terms. These are dense, so f has infinitely many discontinuities in every interval. Yet only finitely many jumps exceed a given σ: π²/(8n²) ≥ σ bounds n, so there are finitely many such points per period/bounded interval.

(6) Integrability criterion (sufficient). Suppose f is bounded, has both one-sided limits at every point, and has only finitely many jumps ≥ σ. Then f is integrable. Sketch, completed on the next page: choose the mesh d so small that
- on every subinterval not containing one of the finitely many big jumps, the oscillation is < σ;
- the total length of the subintervals containing big jumps is arbitrarily small.
This is exactly the condition of §5, namely that the total length of intervals with oscillation > σ can be made arbitrarily small.
errors: No mathematical errors. Several steps are left implicit but are correct: the termwise passage to one-sided limits (justified by uniform convergence), the identification m = n·(odd) of the jumping terms, and Σ_{odd} 1/k² = π²/8.
'Die Zahl der Sprünge … immer endlich' should be read as 'finite in any bounded interval' (f has period 1). This is a harmless implicit restriction.

results.what: f(x)=Σ (nx)/n², with (x) the signed distance to the nearest integer: a bounded function discontinuous exactly at rationals p/(2n) (p odd, lowest terms), with jump π²/(8n²), dense set of discontinuities
results.modern_name: Riemann's function / Riemann's example of an integrable function with dense discontinuities

results.what: Evaluation of the jumps via Σ_{k odd} 1/k² = π²/8
Sufficient condition for integrability: bounded, one-sided limits everywhere, finitely many jumps ≥ σ (regulated-function type criterion), derived from the oscillation criterion
results.modern_name: Riemann integrability of regulated functions; Riemann's oscillation criterion

deep.surprise_reason: This is the fair copy of §6 of Riemann's famous Habilitationsschrift. The example of the integrable function with a dense set of discontinuities is classical and universally attributed to him.

checkable.asserts: (1/(2n²))·π²/8 = π²/(16n²), i.e. the right-limit jump is −π²/(16n²) (expression should be 0)
At x = 1/2 (n = 1) the left jump f(x−0) − f(x) ≈ π²/16 (difference ≈ 0)
Uniform bound |f(x)| ≤ π²/12, giving absolute and uniform convergence

transcription_corrections: The marginal '22.' at top left is an archival/foliation number in pencil, separate from Riemann's page number '24.'.
The transcription matches the image well. 'wenn x = p/2n' should be read as x = p/(2n) with p odd (p denotes an odd number as defined above).
